claimed.text: David Grusch testified under oath on 26 July 2023 that he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme, and that he referred named witnesses to the Intelligence Community Inspector General and to Congress.
Jake Barber, a former special operations pilot, described by name in a January 2025 interview taking part in UAP retrieval operations.

Eric Davis told the New York Times he had briefed Senate Armed Services staff and Senate Intelligence members in October 2019 on retrievals of unexplained objects, and a Defense Department agency in March 2020 about retrievals from off-world vehicles not made on this earth; he said of analysed material that we couldn't make it ourselves, and no public documentation of where it came from or who held it has accompanied the statement.

Garry Nolan said in 2023 that some governments have retrieved artefacts from extraterrestrial craft, and in 2021 that people representing the government and an aerospace corporation approached him about medical harm from supposed interactions with an anomalous craft; neither has been named.
Bob Lazar's 1991 account places nine discs at a claimed site he calls S-4; the board carries that as claimed custody that nothing documented supports.

The private-sector chain is weakly documented: Steve Justice conceded that the ADAM materials were collected from sources with varying levels of chain-of-custody documentation, and the board infers that Harold Puthoff's EarthTech, a private firm outside FOIA, is where documented chains stop, since it has published no results on the samples it held.

The board infers, without a document, that any sustained retrieval capability would sit inside existing mishap-recovery, nuclear-response or foreign materiel units, and that the mix of AAWSAP study topics looks like the profile of an organisation characterising an artefact it already holds.

contested.text: AARO states in Volume I that it found no empirical evidence of reverse engineering of extraterrestrial technology, and the board records that the report addresses and rejects the retrieval claim as well.

The specimens that have been examined came back ordinary or unresolved: Oak Ridge found conventional aluminium alloy, Puthoff wrote in 2012 that tests on one set of samples had produced no anomalous outcome, and the Nolan and Vallee analysis of the Council Bluffs material found no anomalous isotopic values, only an industrial process of unknown origin.

The dismissals are bounded by access: on the board's reading NASA's team saw only unclassified data, so its finding measures its own access, and the new advisory council has no budget and no classified access at all.
Davis's own antigravity survey for DIA, one of the 38 products, concludes that every proposed device faces daunting technical challenges.

Claims drift when retold: UAP Gerb described the Glomar Explorer as leased to Lockheed Martin for twenty years, while the CIA history names Lockheed only as one member of a four-company consortium readying the ship for mining in 1978.

The counter-explanation to Lazar's site comes from two people by unrelated routes: Tom Mahood concludes that there is nothing at Papoose Lake and that S-4 refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range, while T.D. Barnes, a former CIA and NASA engineer who worked at Groom Lake, says the real Site 4 is a remote radar site north of the main facility and that this, not an underground base, is what Lazar referred to.
AARO's Volume I concludes that the Roswell materials were consistent with a Project Mogul balloon and that there is no evidence the government recovered aliens or extraterrestrial material.

lead.text: The legacy programme allegation is the central allegation the board maps: that a multi-decade effort has retrieved craft and material, held them, and tried to reverse-engineer them outside the acknowledged record. It rests on testimony, most prominently David Grusch's sworn account of 2023; AARO says it found no empirical evidence of reverse engineering, and no released AAWSAP-era document records the receipt, transfer or storage of any physical sample.

record.text: Roswell Army Air Field announced on 8 July 1947 that the 509th Bomb Group had come into possession of a flying disc and retracted it the same day; GAO's 1995 search found the base's outgoing messages for 1946 to 1949 destroyed with no disposition authority.

DIA released to Steven Aftergood on 16 January 2019 a list of 38 AATIP research products, given to Congress a year earlier, for work costing about $22 million from 2007 to 2012; the reading room holds them beside the statement of work, contract status briefs and the Reid correspondence.
No released AAWSAP-era document records the receipt, transfer or storage of a physical sample, despite the release of the statement of work, status briefs, the 38 titles and internal memoranda.

AARO's Volume I, released in 2024, states that it found no empirical evidence that the government or private companies reverse-engineered extraterrestrial technology; its January 2026 supplement reports that Oak Ridge found a specimen from Flint Ridge, Ohio consistent with conventional aluminium casting alloys. The DoD Inspector General's UAP evaluation was released in summary on 25 January 2024.

The Army's Ground Vehicle Systems Center signed a cooperative research agreement with To The Stars Academy on 10 October 2019 covering areas such as inertial mass reduction and metamaterials; AARO confirms that the organisation owning alleged crash material agreed in 2019 with the Army to analyse the samples, and in 2020 the Army denied in full a FOIA request for 29 emails of their correspondence.

The CIA's own released history of Project AZORIAN documents a real covert recovery of foreign hardware under commercial cover: a Soviet submarine lost in March 1968 was raised on 8 August 1974 by a system built for the purpose, and the Agency still withholds the other contractors, the technology and the funding.
The CIA's prepublication guidance requires an author whose manuscript is found to contain classified information to return every version for destruction and remove it from their hard drive.

NASA's independent study team reported in September 2023 that it found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin, and the UAP Science Advisory Council announced in June 2026 will receive only unclassified data.

summary.text: The claim has three stages that the board treats as one: retrieval feeds the programme, exploitation is its purpose, and custody runs from the recovery site to wherever the material is kept.

The case for it is testimony: Grusch under oath, named witnesses such as Jake Barber, and scientists such as Eric Davis and Garry Nolan who say they have been told of or approached about recovered material. Each specific allegation has its own topic.

The official answer is AARO's Volume I, which says it found no empirical evidence of reverse engineering by the government or private companies; an Oak Ridge analysis, reported by AARO in January 2026, found one specimen consistent with conventional aluminium alloys.

Between the two sits the custody gap: the released AAWSAP record documents paper in detail and objects not at all, and on the board's reading every documented chain of custody goes dark at a private or classified link.

title: The legacy programme allegation: retrieval, custody and reverse engineering
